paras: The Ku Klux Klan notices in Pittsburgh were printed threats, signed by a self-styled "Klu Klux Klan," that were posted on Black churches and homes in the East Liberty and East End districts of Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, in February 1919, warning Black residents to "stay in their place." Black newspapers from Baltimore to Phoenix carried the story, some presenting it as Klan activity spreading to the North and others printing a denial from R. R. Vann, editor of the Courier, who called the notices "evidently the work of ignorant bums." No violence, arrests or identification of the authors appear in the coverage.

A group signing itself the "Klu Klux Klan" placed signs on many churches and homes in Pittsburgh's East End reading "The War is Over Negroes. Stay in Your Place. If You Don't, We'll Put You There." The signs were printed in red and black ink, with the threats in bold letters. An Associated Press account, as reprinted in the Black press, placed the notices in the East Liberty section, said they had been posted on leading Black churches and sent to the homes of many Black residents, and described "a reign of terror."

According to that report, some Black residents feared for their lives and had not gone out at night since the notices began to appear. Prominent Black citizens were warned that "outrages" committed against Black people in Virginia and Kentucky would be repeated in Pittsburgh unless they "watch their step." A separate dispatch said Black residents were seeking to escape threatened violence and that "representative race people" had taken the matter up with insurance companies because the destruction of property had been threatened.

In a Pittsburgh special dated February 19, the Baltimore Afro-American reported that the rumors of a Klan terrorizing local citizens had been "denied here today." Vann sent the paper a statement that investigation had "proven nothing" and that the notices were "evidently the work of ignorant bums," a phrase the Afro-American's text renders as "huns." The coverage does not say who carried out the investigation, and no report of arrests or of violence following the notices was found.

The story reached the Black press in two forms, a denial built around the Associated Press report and a dispatch that reported the threat on its own terms. The Baltimore Afro-American printed the denial first, on February 21, under the headline "No Klu-Klux Klan In Pittsburgh" and a subhead saying the rumor that the work of Southern "Ruffians" had extended north was denied. On March 1 the Cleveland Advocate ("Klu Klux Klan Threaten Race in Pittsburgh, Pa.") and the Dallas Express ("Klu Klux Fever Spreads to Pittsburgh") ran the other dispatch, dated February 26 and 27, without any denial. The Advocate placed it on a front page with an article saying returning Black soldiers were coming home with "a new vision and grim determination" to obtain the justice they had been promised.

Both versions were still circulating three weeks later. On March 22 the Phoenix Tribune reprinted the threat dispatch without a dateline under "Klu Klux Klan in Pennsylvania," while the Colorado Statesman ran the denial, redated March 4, under "No Ku-Klux Klan in Pittsburgh" and described the Klan as "of southern ill-fame."

The accounts differ on who was behind the notices. The dispatch and the Associated Press report described a Klan-signed campaign that left residents in fear, while Vann's statement treated the Klan signature as unproven and blamed "ignorant bums." The datelines also differ: the Afro-American's special is dated February 19 and refers to an Associated Press report sent the previous Saturday, so the notices predate the February 26 and 27 datelines of the dispatch and the March 4 dateline the Colorado Statesman gave the same denial.

reader.title: Ku Klux Klan notices in Pittsburgh
bases: Printed notices signed 'Klu Klux Klan' threatened Black residents and their property, with no reported violence (A2, A4).

Two differently worded reports, the AP account (A1, A4) and the 'terror stricken' dispatch (A2, A3, A5), agree that threatening notices were posted on Negro churches and homes, and Vann's denial disputes the Klan's role rather than the notices themselves (A1, A4).

accounts.label: Associated Press report (as quoted in the Black press)
accounts.gist: A self-styled Klan spread 'a reign of terror' in East Liberty with notices on Negro churches and mailed to homes; some Negroes stayed in at night and prominent Negroes were warned Virginia and Kentucky outrages would be duplicated.

accounts.label: Pittsburgh dispatch (Feb. 26/27)
accounts.gist: Terror-stricken East End Negroes sought escape from threatened violence by a gang signing itself the Klan; race representatives went to insurance companies over threatened property destruction; signs in red and black ink.

accounts.label: Courier editor R. R. Vann
accounts.gist: Investigation proved nothing; the notices were evidently the work of 'ignorant bums,' and the Klan rumor was denied.

framing.detail: Cleveland Advocate headlined 'Klu Klux Klan Threaten Race in Pittsburgh, Pa.' and the Dallas Express 'Klu Klux Fever Spreads to Pittsburgh,' printing the threat without any denial.
The Afro-American ('No Klu-Klux Klan In Pittsburgh') and Colorado Statesman ('No Ku-Klux Klan in Pittsburgh,' the Klan 'of southern ill-fame') led with the denial while quoting the AP report in full.
Phoenix Tribune reprinted the threat dispatch without dateline or comment as 'Klu Klux Klan in Pennsylvania.'

versions.value: AP report sent the Saturday before Feb. 19 (special dated Feb. 19)

conflicts.note: The Afro-American's Feb. 21 report shows the notices were known by mid-February; the later datelines are transmission or reprint dates, and the Colorado Statesman's March 4 text repeats the Feb. 19 denial.

versions.value: A gang or self-styled Klan spreading 'a reign of terror'
No Klan; 'evidently the work of ignorant bums,' investigation proved nothing

conflicts.note: Vann's statement disputes that an organized Klan was at work, not that the notices were posted.

record_check.dossier: Notices were reported by an AP dispatch sent before Feb. 19 (by mid-February 1919); Feb. 26 is a later dispatch dateline.
Threat, including threatened property destruction; no violence reported.
Unidentified group signing as 'Klu Klux Klan'; Courier editor Vann called it the work of 'ignorant bums.'
5 Black-press articles; the first is the Baltimore Afro-American of 1919-02-21.

info: Notices appeared before the AP report sent out the Saturday before Feb. 19, 1919, i.e. by mid-February; later datelines (Feb. 26, Feb. 27, March 4) are dispatch dates
East Liberty section (AP) / East End (dispatch) of Pittsburgh
Negro residents of the district; notices on Negro churches and homes; prominent Negro citizens warned
A 'gang' or 'self-styled' Ku Klux Klan signing itself 'Klu Klux Klan'; unidentified; Vann called them 'ignorant bums'
